title: Education's Ambulance-at-the-Bottom Problem
author: Dale Chu
summary: Dale Chu applies the classic 'fence at the top of the cliff versus ambulance at the bottom' metaphor to K-12 policy design, arguing that American schooling systematically defaults to crisis response over prevention across multiple domains, accountability that doesn't kick in until third grade despite conditions forming earlier, foreign-language instruction beginning too late in high school to achieve real proficiency, and discipline systems that only intervene once behavior has already escalated over months. His central explanation for this pattern is not incompetence but a structural bias in how success and failure get measured: prevented problems are inherently invisible and uncountable, while crises that get responded to are visible and creditable, a dynamic he captures with Mitch Daniels's line 'dogs don't bark at parked cars.' Chu compounds this measurement bias with an institutional inertia argument, borrowed from his former boss Tony Bennett, that traditional school systems are organized around adult comfort and predictability rather than child outcomes, making the short-term disruption of preventive change feel costlier than the long-term, harder-to-see cost of continued crisis response. He is careful not to argue prevention can replace all intervention, noting Tier II and Tier III supports remain necessary, and reframes the real policy question as one of timing: not just what schools should achieve, but when they need to act to make that achievement possible at all.
points: Chu's structural explanation for chronic under-prevention is a measurement-bias argument: because prevented problems generate no crisis to point to as evidence, while crisis interventions are visible and creditable, education data systems inherently undercount prevention's value, a dynamic he captures via Mitch Daniels's 'dogs don't bark at parked cars.'

He identifies third-grade reading accountability as a specific policy example of the ambulance-at-the-bottom pattern: schools face no accountability for reading outcomes until the end of third grade even though the conditions shaping reading success form well before that checkpoint.

His discipline analysis reframes the standard suspension-rate debate: by the time a student is suspended or expelled, the school is typically responding to behavior that escalated over months or years, meaning the relevant policy failure occurred earlier, in the absence of established routines and expectations, not at the moment of suspension itself.

Citing his former boss Tony Bennett, Chu names the institutional root cause directly: 'the traditional system is organized around adult comfort rather than what's best for children,' explaining why schools rationally resist visible, disruptive preventive change in favor of familiar crisis response.

He explicitly avoids an all-or-nothing prevention argument, stating 'sometimes the ambulance is exactly what's needed' and that Tier II/Tier III interventions matter, reframing the real policy task as sequencing, deciding what must happen early versus what can reasonably wait, rather than eliminating responsive supports altogether.
quotes: There's an old adage that it's better to build a sturdy fence at the top of a cliff than station an ambulance at the bottom.
Schools aren't held accountable for reading and math outcomes until the end of third grade, even though many of the conditions that shape student success take hold well before then.
By the time a student has misbehaved himself into suspension, expulsion, or involvement with law enforcement, the school is often dealing with behavior that has escalated over months or even years.

A student who learns to read well in the early grades may never need tutoring, but there is no obvious crisis to point to as evidence that the early instruction worked... As Mitch Daniels often says, "Dogs don't bark at parked cars.
My former boss, Tony Bennett, often talked about how the traditional system is organized around adult comfort rather than what's best for children.
The point isn't that every problem can be headed off. Sometimes the ambulance is exactly what's needed. Tier II and Tier III supports matter.
The alternative is to keep asking schools to solve problems after they've become intractable.
